A controversy at Emory University over graffiti promoting Donald Trump led to some predictably inaccurate media reports.

archive.is

The last paragraph (which is quoted from the Emory source paper) disproves the rest of the article.

The idea that the event was falsely reported hinges on her (the authors) pointing out that "safe spaces" wasn't referenced. I don't think anyone reading or watching the news reports that mocked the students heard "safe spaces' and thought "designated locations on campus". The term "safe space" is typically used in a mocking manner to begin with. College is a place where thoughts are supposed to be challenged, therefore "safe spaces" are considered a joke all around.

WHAT'S FALSE: "Emergency counseling" was offered to or demanded by students; Emory students complained that their "safe spaces" had been violated; students were afraid of or traumatized by the chalk markings.

Similarly, I don't think anyone aside from the author thought the students were literally afraid of the chalk jumping off the concrete and attacking them. Using literal definitions to mark a story "Mostly False" when the stories were using artistic or figurative language seems a bit disingenuous.
